name: Apple

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Skin should be vibrant and free of bruises or wrinkles. A slight sheen indicates freshness.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should feel firm and heavy for its size. Soft spots mean it is past its peak.

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: A sweet, fruity aroma near the stem end indicates ripeness. No smell often means it was picked too early.

ripenessTips.title: Check stem
ripenessTips.description: The stem should be intact. A missing stem lets air in and speeds spoilage.

funFact: There are over 7,500 apple varieties grown worldwide, though most grocery stores carry only about 5 to 10.
storageTip: Store in the crisper drawer of the refrigerator for up to 6 weeks. Keep away from other produce, as apples release ethylene gas that speeds ripening.

name: Apricot

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Should be uniformly golden-orange with no green patches. A slight blush of red is fine.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Gently press the fruit: it should give slightly but not feel mushy. Too firm means it is underripe.

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: Ripe apricots have a sweet, floral fragrance. If there is no scent, they are not ready.

funFact: Apricots were cultivated in China over 4,000 years ago before traveling along the Silk Road to the Mediterranean.
storageTip: Ripen at room temperature stem-side down, then refrigerate for up to 5 days. Do not wash until ready to eat.

name: Avocado

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Gently squeeze without pressing fingertips in. It should yield to gentle pressure when ripe.

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Hass avocados turn dark purplish-black when ripe. Green varieties stay green, so rely on feel.

ripenessTips.title: Check stem
ripenessTips.description: Flick off the small stem cap. If it comes off easily and is green underneath, it is ripe. Brown underneath means overripe.

ripenessTips.title: Heft
ripenessTips.description: A ripe avocado should feel heavy for its size, indicating it still has moisture.

funFact: Avocados do not ripen on the tree; farmers can leave them hanging for months as a form of natural storage.
storageTip: Ripen on the counter in 2 to 5 days. To speed it up, place in a paper bag with a banana. Once ripe, refrigerate for up to 3 days.

name: Banana

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Yellow with small brown freckles is the sweet spot. Fully green means underripe; mostly brown means best for baking.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should be firm but not hard. The peel should give slightly under gentle pressure.

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: A ripe banana has a sweet, pleasant fragrance at the stem end.

funFact: Bananas are technically berries, while strawberries are not; botanists classify them based on seed and flower structure.
storageTip: Store at room temperature until ripe. To slow ripening, wrap the stem in plastic wrap. Refrigerating turns the peel brown but the fruit inside stays good for several days.

name: Blueberry

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Should be deep indigo-blue with a silvery-white bloom (natural waxy coating). Red or green tinges mean underripe.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should be plump and firm. Squeeze the container gently; berries should move freely, not stick together in clumps.

ripenessTips.title: Check container
ripenessTips.description: Flip the container and look for juice stains or crushed berries at the bottom, which indicate damage.

funFact: Blueberries are one of the only natural foods that are truly blue; the color comes from anthocyanin pigments.
storageTip: Do not wash until ready to eat. Store in the refrigerator in a single layer on a paper towel for up to 10 days. Freeze on a sheet pan before transferring to a bag.

name: Cantaloupe

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: The rind under the netting should be golden or cream-colored, not green. The blossom end should have a slight give.

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: Sniff the stem end. A ripe cantaloupe has a sweet, musky aroma. No scent means it is underripe.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should feel heavy for its size. The stem end should be slightly indented, meaning it slipped off the vine when ripe.

ripenessTips.title: Listen
ripenessTips.description: Tap the outside. A deep, low sound indicates the flesh is dense and juicy.

funFact: What Americans call cantaloupe is actually a muskmelon; true cantaloupes have a smoother rind and are more common in Europe.
storageTip: Ripen at room temperature until fragrant, then refrigerate and eat within 3 to 5 days. Cut melon should be wrapped and eaten within 2 days.

name: Cherry

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Should be deeply colored: dark red to almost black for sweet varieties, bright red for sour. Avoid pale or shriveled cherries.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should be plump and firm with glossy, taut skin. Soft or wrinkled cherries are past their prime.

ripenessTips.title: Check stem
ripenessTips.description: Green, flexible stems indicate freshness. Brown, brittle stems mean they have been sitting too long.

funFact: Cherry trees are related to roses, almonds, and peaches, all belonging to the Prunus genus in the Rosaceae family.
storageTip: Store unwashed in a single layer in the refrigerator for up to a week. Bring to room temperature before eating for best flavor. Freeze pitted cherries on a sheet pan.

name: Cranberry

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Should be deep red with a glossy, smooth surface. Pale or white berries are underripe.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: A ripe cranberry is firm and bounces when dropped on a hard surface. Soft berries should be discarded.

ripenessTips.title: Inspect
ripenessTips.description: Check the bag for moisture or crushed berries. Dry, firm berries in a clean bag will last the longest.

funFact: Cranberries have small air pockets inside, which is why they float in water and can be wet-harvested by flooding the bogs.
storageTip: Refrigerate in their original bag for up to 2 months. Freeze in a single layer, then bag them; frozen cranberries last up to a year.

name: Fig

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Should be plump and slightly drooping at the neck. Color depends on variety: deep purple, green, or brown.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: A ripe fig yields to gentle pressure like a ripe peach. Rock-hard figs were picked too early and will not ripen well.

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: Should smell sweet and jammy. A sour or fermented smell means it is overripe.

funFact: Figs are technically inverted flowers; the tiny seeds inside are the actual fruits of the plant.
storageTip: Figs are highly perishable. Store on a plate lined with paper towel in the refrigerator and eat within 2 to 3 days of purchase.

name: Grape

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Should be plump with consistent color. A whitish bloom on the surface is natural and indicates freshness.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Pick up the bunch and shake gently. A few grapes may fall, but many dropping indicates they are past peak.

ripenessTips.title: Check stem
ripenessTips.description: The stem should be green and flexible. A brown, dry, or brittle stem means old grapes.

funFact: A single grapevine can produce enough fruit to make about 10 bottles of wine, and some vines live for over 100 years.
storageTip: Store unwashed in a ventilated bag or container in the refrigerator for up to 2 weeks. Wash just before eating.

name: Grapefruit

ripenessTips.title: Heft
ripenessTips.description: Pick it up: a ripe grapefruit is surprisingly heavy for its size, indicating high juice content.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should be firm but springy with smooth, thin skin. Thick, puffy skin often means less juice inside.

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Color varies by variety but should be vibrant. Slight green tinge on otherwise colored fruit is fine.

funFact: Grapefruit got its name because it grows in clusters on the tree, similar to how grapes grow in bunches.
storageTip: Store at room temperature for about a week, or refrigerate for up to 6 weeks. Bring to room temperature before eating for the juiciest flavor.

name: Kiwi

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Press gently with your thumb. A ripe kiwi gives slightly, like a ripe pear. Rock-hard means it needs more time.

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: The fuzzy brown skin should be intact without wrinkles, dark spots, or mold.

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: A ripe kiwi has a light, fruity fragrance. A strong or fermented smell indicates it is overripe.

funFact: Kiwis were originally called Chinese gooseberries; New Zealand growers renamed them after their national bird for marketing appeal.
storageTip: Ripen at room temperature away from sunlight. Once ripe, store in the refrigerator for up to 4 weeks. To speed ripening, place in a bag with a banana.

name: Lemon

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Should be bright, vibrant yellow with smooth, fine-grained skin. Pale or greenish lemons tend to be more acidic.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Choose lemons that are firm but give slightly. Thin-skinned lemons yield more juice than thick-skinned ones.

ripenessTips.title: Heft
ripenessTips.description: A juicy lemon feels heavy for its size. Lightweight lemons have dried out inside.

funFact: Lemon juice is a natural preservative; its citric acid prevents cut fruits like apples and avocados from browning.
storageTip: Store at room temperature for a week, or in a sealed bag in the refrigerator for up to a month. A whole lemon kept in water in the fridge stays juicy even longer.

name: Mango

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: Sniff the stem end. A ripe mango has a strong, sweet, fruity aroma. No smell means it needs more time.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should yield gently to pressure, like a ripe avocado. Very firm is underripe; mushy is overripe.

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Color depends on variety and is not the best indicator. Focus on feel and smell instead. Avoid any with wrinkled or oozing skin.

funFact: Mangoes are the most consumed fruit in the world, with over 400 varieties grown across tropical regions.
storageTip: Ripen at room temperature until fragrant and slightly soft. Once ripe, refrigerate for up to 5 days. Cut mango can be frozen for smoothies.

name: Orange

ripenessTips.title: Heft
ripenessTips.description: A heavy orange means more juice. Compare similarly sized oranges and pick the heaviest one.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should be firm with smooth, thin skin. Puffy or spongy skin usually means less juice and more pith.

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: A slight green tinge does not mean unripe; oranges sometimes regreen. Uniform shape is a better indicator of quality.

funFact: The color orange was actually named after the fruit, not the other way around; before that, English speakers called the color 'geoluhread' (yellow-red).
storageTip: Store at room temperature for about a week, or in the refrigerator for up to 3 weeks. Roll on the counter before juicing to get more juice out.

name: Peach

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: A ripe peach has a strong, sweet fragrance you can smell from arm's length. No scent likely means no flavor.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should give slightly to gentle pressure, especially along the seam. Avoid rock-hard or mushy fruit.

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: The background color (not the blush) tells ripeness. It should be golden or creamy, not green.

funFact: Despite being called Persian apples in many languages, peaches originated in China where they have been cultivated for over 8,000 years.
storageTip: Ripen at room temperature stem-side down. Once ripe, refrigerate for up to 5 days. Cold peaches lose some flavor, so bring back to room temperature before eating.

name: Pear

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Press gently near the stem. If it yields slightly, it is ripe. Pears ripen from the inside out, so the flesh is ready before the skin shows it.

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Color change varies by type. Bartlett pears turn yellow; Bosc stay brown. Check the neck, not the body.

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: A sweet, floral fragrance near the stem means it is ready. If there is no aroma, it needs more time.

funFact: Pears are one of the few fruits that ripen better off the tree; left on the branch they develop a gritty texture from stone cells.
storageTip: Buy firm and ripen at room temperature for a few days. Once the neck yields to gentle pressure, refrigerate for up to 5 days.

name: Persimmon

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Should be deep orange to reddish-orange with glossy skin. Green patches indicate immaturity.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Hachiya persimmons should be jelly-soft when ripe. Fuyu types can be eaten when still firm, like an apple.

ripenessTips.title: Check leaves
ripenessTips.description: The calyx (leaf cap) should be flat against the fruit and green. A dried, pulling-away calyx means it is old.

funFact: Unripe Hachiya persimmons contain high levels of tannins that cause an intense, mouth-puckering astringency that vanishes when fully ripe.
storageTip: Ripen Hachiyas at room temperature until very soft, which can take a week or more. Fuyu types store for a few weeks in the fridge. Freeze puree for baking.

name: Pineapple

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: Sniff the base. A strong, sweet, tropical aroma means it is ripe. No smell means bland fruit; fermented smell means overripe.

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Should be golden-yellow from the base up. More yellow means sweeter. Leaves should be green, not brown.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should feel firm but give slightly when pressed. A leaf from the center crown should pull out with gentle effort when ripe.

ripenessTips.title: Heft
ripenessTips.description: Should feel heavy for its size, meaning it is full of juice.

funFact: A pineapple is actually a cluster of 100 to 200 individual berries fused together around a central core.
storageTip: A pineapple will not ripen further after picking; it only gets softer. Store upside down at room temperature for 1 to 2 days to distribute sweetness. Refrigerate cut pineapple for up to 5 days.

name: Pomegranate

ripenessTips.title: Heft
ripenessTips.description: Should feel surprisingly heavy; the weight comes from juice-filled arils inside.

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Skin should be deep red and taut. Slight angularity of the sides (not perfectly round) means the arils are full.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: The skin should be firm and leathery, not soft or cracked. Small scratches on the surface do not affect quality.

funFact: A single pomegranate contains about 600 to 800 arils (seed pods), each wrapped in a jewel-like sac of juice.
storageTip: Whole pomegranates last up to 2 months in the refrigerator. Store arils in an airtight container in the fridge for up to a week, or freeze them for months.

name: Strawberry

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Should be uniformly bright red from tip to stem with no white or green patches. White shoulders mean underripe.

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: The most reliable test: ripe strawberries have a strong, sweet berry fragrance. No smell means no flavor.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should be firm but not hard. Avoid soft, mushy, or leaking berries.

ripenessTips.title: Check cap
ripenessTips.description: The green cap should be bright and fresh-looking, firmly attached. Wilted caps mean they were picked days ago.

funFact: Strawberries are the only fruit that wears its seeds on the outside, with about 200 tiny seeds on each berry.
storageTip: Do not wash until ready to eat. Store in a single layer on paper towels in the refrigerator for 3 to 5 days. Moldy berries should be removed immediately as mold spreads fast.

name: Watermelon

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Check the field spot where it rested on the ground. A creamy yellow spot indicates ripeness; white means underripe.

ripenessTips.title: Listen
ripenessTips.description: Knock on it. A ripe watermelon produces a deep, hollow sound. A dull thud means it may be overripe.

ripenessTips.title: Heft
ripenessTips.description: Should feel very heavy for its size. Watermelons are 92 percent water, so weight means juiciness.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: The rind should be hard and resist scratching with a fingernail. A slightly bumpy surface texture is normal.

funFact: Watermelon is both a fruit and a vegetable; it belongs to the cucumber and squash family (Cucurbitaceae).
storageTip: Store whole at room temperature for up to 2 weeks. Cut watermelon should be refrigerated in an airtight container and eaten within 5 days.

name: Artichoke

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Leaves should be tightly packed, firm, and green. Spreading or browning leaves mean it is past its prime.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should feel heavy and dense for its size. Squeeze it: a fresh artichoke squeaks slightly.

ripenessTips.title: Listen
ripenessTips.description: Squeeze the artichoke near your ear. A fresh one makes a squeaking sound as the leaves press together.

funFact: The part of the artichoke we eat is actually an immature flower bud; if left unharvested, it blooms into a large, purple thistle.
storageTip: Store unwashed in a plastic bag in the refrigerator for up to a week. Sprinkle a few drops of water in the bag to keep them hydrated.

name: Asparagus

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Tips should be tightly closed and compact, not flowering or mushy. Stalks should be bright green or purple.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Stalks should be firm and straight, snapping cleanly when bent. Limp asparagus is old.

ripenessTips.title: Check base
ripenessTips.description: The cut ends should look fresh and moist, not dried out, woody, or excessively white.

funFact: Asparagus is one of the fastest growing vegetables, capable of growing up to 10 inches in a single day under ideal conditions.
storageTip: Treat like cut flowers: trim the ends and stand upright in a jar with an inch of water, covered loosely with a plastic bag. Refrigerate and use within 3 to 5 days.

name: Beetroot

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Should be deep, rich color with smooth skin. Avoid beets with scales, bruises, or soft wet spots.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should be very firm and hard, like a rock. Soft beets are old. Smaller beets tend to be sweeter and more tender.

ripenessTips.title: Check greens
ripenessTips.description: If greens are still attached, they should be vibrant and not wilted. Fresh greens indicate a freshly harvested beet.

funFact: Beets were originally cultivated for their greens only; eating the root did not become popular until the 1500s in Germany.
storageTip: Remove greens immediately as they draw moisture from the root. Store unwashed roots in a plastic bag in the refrigerator for up to 3 weeks. Cook greens separately within 2 days.

name: Bell Pepper

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Should have vibrant, glossy skin with no wrinkles or dull patches. Color should be uniform throughout.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should be firm with thick walls that do not flex easily when pressed. Avoid soft spots or thin walls.

ripenessTips.title: Heft
ripenessTips.description: A heavy pepper has thick, juicy walls. Lighter ones tend to have thinner flesh.

ripenessTips.title: Check stem
ripenessTips.description: The stem should be bright green and firmly attached. A brown or withered stem signals age.

funFact: Green bell peppers are actually unripe; if left on the plant they turn yellow, then orange, then red, getting sweeter at each stage.
storageTip: Store unwashed in the crisper drawer for up to 2 weeks. Cut peppers should be stored in an airtight container and used within 3 days.

name: Broccoli

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Florets should be tightly closed and dark green to blue-green. Yellowing florets mean it is starting to flower and past peak.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: The head should be firm and the stalk should feel crisp when snapped. Rubbery stalks indicate old broccoli.

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: Fresh broccoli has a mild, slightly green scent. A strong, cabbage-like odor means it is getting old.

funFact: Broccoli is a human invention, bred by Italian farmers from wild cabbage plants starting in the 6th century BCE.
storageTip: Store unwashed in a loose plastic bag in the refrigerator for up to 5 days. Do not seal tightly as broccoli needs some airflow. Do not wash before storing.

name: Brussels Sprouts

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Should be bright green with tightly packed leaves. Avoid any with black spots or yellowing outer leaves.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should be firm and compact. Loose or puffy sprouts will be bitter and have a cabbage-like taste.

ripenessTips.title: Check size
ripenessTips.description: Smaller sprouts (about 1 inch) tend to be sweeter and more tender than larger ones.

funFact: Brussels sprouts taste less bitter after a frost because the cold triggers the plant to convert starches into sugars as a natural antifreeze.
storageTip: Store in a bag in the refrigerator for up to a week. If still on the stalk, they keep even longer. Trim and halve right before cooking.

name: Cabbage

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should feel very heavy and solid when picked up. The head should be compact with no give when squeezed.

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Outer leaves should be vibrant and fresh, not wilted, yellowed, or slimy. Check the stem end for signs of browning.

ripenessTips.title: Heft
ripenessTips.description: Compare cabbages of similar size; the heavier one is denser and fresher.

funFact: Cabbage was one of the first vegetables cultivated by Europeans, and sauerkraut was reportedly fed to workers building the Great Wall of China.
storageTip: Whole, unwashed cabbage will keep in the crisper drawer for up to 2 months. Once cut, wrap tightly in plastic wrap and use within 5 days.

name: Carrot

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Should be bright orange with smooth skin. Cracks, green shoulders, or forking indicate poor growing conditions.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should be firm and rigid, not bendy or limp. A bendable carrot has lost its moisture.

ripenessTips.title: Check greens
ripenessTips.description: If tops are attached, they should be bright green and feathery. Wilted tops mean the carrot is not fresh.

funFact: Carrots were originally purple and yellow; the orange variety was developed in the Netherlands in the 17th century.
storageTip: Remove greens immediately as they pull moisture from the root. Store in a sealed bag in the crisper drawer for up to 3 weeks. Limp carrots can be revived by soaking in ice water.

name: Cauliflower

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: The head should be creamy white (or uniformly colored for purple/green varieties) with no brown or dark spots.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should be heavy and firm with compact, tightly packed florets. Loose, spreading florets indicate over-maturity.

ripenessTips.title: Check leaves
ripenessTips.description: The surrounding leaves should be green and crisp, hugging the head. Wilted or yellow leaves mean it is old.

funFact: Cauliflower is available in purple, orange, and green varieties, each with slightly different nutritional profiles and flavors.
storageTip: Store whole, unwashed, stem-side up in a loosely closed bag in the refrigerator for up to a week. Cut florets last about 4 days.

name: Corn

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Through the husk, the ear should feel plump with kernels you can feel from top to bottom. Gaps mean poor pollination.

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: The silk at the top should be brown and slightly sticky, not dry and black. Green husks should be tightly wrapped.

ripenessTips.title: Check kernels
ripenessTips.description: Peel back a small section of husk. Kernels should be plump and release milky liquid when pierced. Clear liquid means underripe.

funFact: Corn always has an even number of rows on each ear, typically between 12 and 16, due to the way the kernels develop in pairs.
storageTip: Eat as soon as possible; corn starts converting sugar to starch within hours of picking. Store in the husk in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Do not shuck until ready to cook.

name: Cucumber

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Should be dark green and uniform with no yellowing, which indicates over-maturity and bitter seeds.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should be very firm from end to end. Soft ends mean the cucumber is aging and the inside is getting mushy.

ripenessTips.title: Check size
ripenessTips.description: Medium-sized cucumbers have the best flavor and texture. Very large ones tend to be seedy and bitter.

funFact: Cucumbers are 96 percent water, making them one of the most hydrating foods available.
storageTip: Wrap individually in a paper towel and store in a loose bag in the refrigerator for up to a week. Keep away from tomatoes and bananas which speed deterioration.

name: Eggplant

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Should have smooth, glossy, taut skin with consistent deep purple color. Dull or wrinkled skin means it is old.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Press gently with your thumb. It should spring back. If the indent stays, it is overripe. If rock-hard, it is underripe.

ripenessTips.title: Heft
ripenessTips.description: Should feel heavy for its size. Lightweight eggplants can be spongy and bitter inside.

ripenessTips.title: Check cap
ripenessTips.description: The green calyx and stem should look fresh, not dried or moldy.

funFact: Eggplants are technically berries and members of the nightshade family, along with tomatoes, potatoes, and tobacco.
storageTip: Store at room temperature and use within 2 days, or refrigerate in the crisper drawer for up to 5 days. Cold temperatures can damage the texture if stored too long.

name: Green Beans

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Should be bright green with a smooth surface. Avoid beans with visible bulges from oversized seeds inside.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should snap cleanly when bent in half. If they bend without breaking, they are old and rubbery.

ripenessTips.title: Check size
ripenessTips.description: Slender, young beans are more tender and flavorful than thick, mature ones with prominent seeds.

funFact: Green beans were one of the first New World foods to be adopted in Europe after Spanish explorers brought them back in the 16th century.
storageTip: Store unwashed in a plastic bag in the crisper drawer for up to 7 days. To freeze, blanch for 3 minutes first, then ice-bath and dry before bagging.

name: Kale

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Leaves should be deeply colored (dark green to blue-green) and crisp with no yellowing or brown spots.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Leaves should feel sturdy and firm, not limp or slimy. Smaller leaves are more tender for salads.

ripenessTips.title: Check stems
ripenessTips.description: Stems should be moist at the cut end and firm. Dried-out or slimy stems mean old kale.

funFact: Kale becomes sweeter after exposure to frost, similar to Brussels sprouts, as the plant converts starch to sugar to protect its cells.
storageTip: Wrap in a damp paper towel and store in a loose bag in the refrigerator for up to a week. Do not wash before storing as moisture accelerates decay.

name: Peas

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Pods should be bright green, plump, and slightly shiny. Dull, yellowish, or dry pods are past their prime.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: For shelling peas, the pods should feel full and firm. For sugar snaps and snow peas, they should be crisp and flat.

ripenessTips.title: Listen
ripenessTips.description: Snap a pod in half: it should make a clean, audible snap. A limp bend means they are old.

funFact: Gregor Mendel used peas to discover the fundamental laws of genetics in the 1860s, making the humble pea foundational to modern biology.
storageTip: Eat as quickly as possible; like corn, peas begin converting sugar to starch immediately after picking. Refrigerate in a bag for up to 3 days. Freeze quickly if not eating right away.

name: Pumpkin

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Should be a deep, uniform orange (or color typical for variety) with no soft spots, cuts, or mold.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: The rind should be very hard and resist a thumbnail pressed into it. Soft rind means it is not fully mature.

ripenessTips.title: Listen
ripenessTips.description: Knock on it. A ripe pumpkin sounds hollow, similar to a drum.

ripenessTips.title: Check stem
ripenessTips.description: A dry, corky stem indicates maturity. Never carry a pumpkin by its stem, as it can break off and invite rot.

funFact: Pumpkins are about 90 percent water and are technically a fruit because they develop from the flowering part of the plant and contain seeds.
storageTip: Cure in a warm spot for 10 days, then store in a cool, dry place for up to 3 months. Cut pumpkin can be refrigerated for a week or frozen for months.

name: Radish

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Should be brightly colored with smooth, unblemished skin. Avoid cracked or oversized radishes, which may be pithy inside.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should be rock-hard and firm. A spongy or soft radish has a woody, hollow center.

ripenessTips.title: Check greens
ripenessTips.description: If greens are attached, they should look fresh and perky, not slimy or yellow.

funFact: Radishes were among the first European crops planted in the Americas and were even grown by astronauts on the International Space Station.
storageTip: Remove greens right away and store radishes in a bag in the refrigerator for up to 2 weeks. To restore crispness, soak in ice water for 30 minutes.

name: Spinach

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Leaves should be vibrant dark green and crisp. Yellow, wilted, or slimy leaves indicate age.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Leaves should feel springy and resilient, not limp or soggy. Thicker leaves hold up better in cooking.

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: Should have a fresh, earthy scent. A sour or off smell means it has started to decay.

funFact: Spinach loses about 90 percent of its volume when cooked because the heat breaks down the cell walls and releases all the water stored inside.
storageTip: Store in a bag lined with paper towels in the refrigerator for up to 5 days. Do not wash before storing. Excess moisture is the top cause of quick spoilage.

name: Sweet Potato

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Skin should be smooth and uniform in color with no cracks, soft spots, or sprouts.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should be very firm throughout. Any soft or mushy areas indicate rot that will spread.

ripenessTips.title: Check size
ripenessTips.description: Choose medium-sized sweet potatoes for the best texture. Very large ones can be fibrous and less sweet.

funFact: Despite the name, sweet potatoes are not related to regular potatoes at all; they belong to the morning glory family.
storageTip: Store in a cool, dark, well-ventilated place (not the refrigerator) for up to a month. Cold temperatures convert starches to sugars and alter the texture.

name: Tomato

ripenessTips.title: Smell
ripenessTips.description: Sniff near the stem. A ripe tomato has a rich, earthy, sweet tomato smell. No smell usually means no flavor.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should give slightly to gentle pressure but bounce back. Hard means underripe; very soft means overripe.

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Color should be deep and uniform for the variety. The bottom (blossom end) should be the same color as the sides.

ripenessTips.title: Heft
ripenessTips.description: A ripe tomato is heavy for its size, indicating juiciness and dense flesh.

funFact: Tomatoes were once considered poisonous in Europe because wealthy people who ate them from pewter plates got sick from the lead leaching into the acidic juice.
storageTip: Never refrigerate unripe tomatoes; cold kills the flavor enzymes permanently. Store stem-side down at room temperature. Once fully ripe, eat within a day or two.

name: Zucchini

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Should be dark green and glossy with no nicks, soft spots, or shriveled ends.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should be firm from end to end. Soft spots or sponginess indicate it is old or was damaged.

ripenessTips.title: Check size
ripenessTips.description: Smaller zucchini (6 to 8 inches) have the best flavor and texture. Large ones are watery and seedy.

funFact: A single zucchini plant can produce 6 to 10 pounds of fruit in a season, which is why gardeners are famously known for giving away their surplus.
storageTip: Store unwashed in a perforated bag in the crisper drawer for up to a week. Do not cut until ready to use, as exposed flesh deteriorates quickly.

name: Lettuce

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: Leaves should be crisp, vibrant, and free from brown edges, slime, or wilting. Avoid heads with a pinkish tint on the ribs.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should feel springy and light for its size. A head that feels too dense or heavy may be over-mature and bitter.

ripenessTips.title: Check base
ripenessTips.description: The cut end at the base should look fresh and white, not brown or dried out.

funFact: Ancient Egyptians first cultivated lettuce not for eating but for the oil from its seeds; it was later adopted as a food crop by the Greeks and Romans.
storageTip: Wrap in a damp paper towel and store in a loose bag in the crisper drawer for up to a week. Keep away from apples and bananas which cause browning.

name: Leek

ripenessTips.title: Look
ripenessTips.description: The white and light green portion should be clean, firm, and long. Dark green tops should be vibrant, not yellowed.

ripenessTips.title: Feel
ripenessTips.description: Should be firm and crisp from root to top. Avoid leeks that feel soft, slimy, or rubbery.

ripenessTips.title: Check size
ripenessTips.description: Medium-sized leeks (about 1 to 1.5 inches in diameter) are more tender than very thick ones, which can be tough.

funFact: The leek is the national emblem of Wales; legend says Welsh soldiers wore leeks on their helmets to distinguish themselves in battle.
storageTip: Store untrimmed and unwashed in a loose plastic bag in the refrigerator for up to 2 weeks. Do not trim until ready to cook, and rinse thoroughly between layers to remove trapped dirt.
